items.title: John LaPorta interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 13, 1996
items.q: Of course I had problems playing with white groups because my influences were black when I was young. When I first started hearing records around the age of sixteen, seventeen, I got into Lester Young and Duke and you know their music.

ctx.x: Well there certainly was. A good example would be Dixieland music. I never realized until I made a study, I wanted to do a New Orleans concert at the school after being there for twenty-five years and never having seen one at Berklee, I guess it was a modern school for that time, I decided to do a New Orleans concert. And the students really loved it because it was so different from what they heard there. But in the process of preparing for it, I got to realize that the thing about feeling music in four-four…

evident qualities. Of course I had problems playing with white groups because my influences were black when I was young. When I first started hearing records around the age of sixteen, seventeen, I got into Lester Young and Duke and you know their music. Whenever I went to a white session and sat in, of course they were playing Dixieland music, and they’d accuse me of playing wrong notes and everything else, it was what I heard. And then I’d play in a black session and nobody seemed to be bugged about the…

Well it’s served you pretty well. I’m interested in, you brought up Charles Mingus and I know you did some significant work with him, in fact we have this piece of work here. And you got along pretty well with him then.
